solution:
Section 1.3 opens "Crystalline solids are further classified into four categories : ionic solids, covalent network solids, molecular solids and metallic solids." So a molecular solid is, by the chapter's own classification, one of the four kinds of **crystalline** solid — §1.3.3 lists \(\mathrm{Cl_2}\), \(\mathrm{CH_4}\), \(\mathrm{H_2}\), \(\mathrm{CO_2}\), \(\mathrm{O_2}\) as substances that "on solidfication give molecular **crystals**".

Why the other three fail: *amorphous solids* (§1.2.2) are the opposite category — randomly arranged particles, no long-range order, no sharp melting point — and molecular crystals are not listed there; *ionic solids* (§1.3.1) are built from charged ions held by coulomb force, whereas the constituent particles of a molecular solid are neutral molecules; *metallic solids* (§1.3.4) are formed by atoms of a metallic element held by metallic bonds. Each of those names a sibling class, not a property of molecular solids.

Hence molecular solids are crystalline solids.

Section 1.9.5 states that "An n-type semiconductor is obtained by adding group 15 element to intrinsic semiconductor which belongs to group 14", and names the dopants explicitly: "Si or Ge doped with group 15 elements such as P, As, Sb or Bi is an n-type semiconductor." Arsenic is a group 15 element, so Si doped with As is n-type.

Why the other three fail: *pure Si* is an **intrinsic** semiconductor — it is not doped at all, so it is neither n- nor p-type; *Ga* and *In* are group 13 elements, and the same section states that "the Si or Ge doped with group 13 elements like B, Ga or In, is a **p**-type semiconductor", the charge carriers there being holes rather than extra electrons.

Hence Si doped with As is the n-type semiconductor.

Section 1.8.1 (iv) lists the *consequences of Frenkel defect*: "As no ions are missing from the crystal lattice as a whole, the density of solid and its chemical properties remain unchanged" and "The crystal as a whole remains electrically neutral because the equal numbers of cations and anions are present." In a Frenkel defect an ion merely moves from its regular site into an interstitial space — it stays inside the crystal — so the overall electrical neutrality is preserved.

Why the other three fail: neutrality is **not** changed, so the first option contradicts the chapter directly; the density is **not** changed either, because no matter leaves the crystal (contrast the Schottky defect, §1.8.1 (iii), where "the density of the substance decreases"); and "both cation and anion are missing" describes the **Schottky** defect, not the Frenkel defect.

Hence in Frenkel defect the overall electrical neutrality is preserved.

Section 1.7.2 derives the packing efficiency of the bcc lattice and concludes: "Thus, 68% of the total volume in bcc unit lattice is occupied by atoms and 32 % is empty space or void volume." The question asks for the **void** volume, which is therefore 32 %.

Why the other three fail: 68 % is the *occupied* fraction of a bcc cell, not the void; 74 % is the *occupied* fraction of an fcc/ccp/hcp lattice (§1.7.3); 26 % is the *void* fraction of an fcc/ccp/hcp lattice. All three are real numbers from Table 1.4 attached to the wrong quantity or the wrong lattice.

Hence the void volume in a bcc crystal lattice is 32 %.

Table 1.4 gives the coordination number of a bcc lattice as "8 : four in the layer below and four in the layer above". The central particle of a body-centred cube touches all eight corner particles, so its coordination number is 8.

Why the other three fail: 6 is the coordination number of the **simple cubic** lattice (§1.6.2 a — "4 in its own layer, 1 above and 1 below"); 2 and 4 are not coordination numbers of any lattice the chapter discusses — 2 is the number of *particles per bcc unit cell* (§1.5.1 ii) and 4 is the number of *particles per fcc unit cell* (§1.5.1 iii) and also the two-dimensional coordination number of square close packing (§1.6.1 b i). Note that 12, the value for hcp/ccp, is not offered at all.

Hence the coordination number of atoms in a bcc crystal lattice is 8.

[Textbook misprint: TWO of the four options are incorrect statements as printed, so the question does not have a unique answer as it stands. Besides the keyed option, the book also prints "The centres of spheres in octahedral voids are at the apices of a regular tetrahedron" — an octahedral void is surrounded by SIX spheres whose centres lie at the apices of a regular OCTAHEDRON (§1.6.1), and "tetrahedron" there is a misprint for "octahedron". The keyed answer is the claim that N atoms give 2N octahedral voids, because that is the statement the chapter's own Remember box in §1.6.3 directly refutes ("number of tetrahedral voids is 2N and that of octahedral voids is N") and the one this question is set to test.]

The chapter's *Remember* box in §1.6.3 states the rule outright: "If N denotes number of particles, then number of tetrahedral voids is 2N and that of octahedral voids is N." So for N atoms the number of **octahedral** voids is N, not 2N — the option asserting 2N octahedral voids is the incorrect statement.

Checking the others: "Four spheres are involved in the formation of tetrahedral void" agrees with §1.6.1 ("A tetrahedral void is surrounded by four spheres"), so it is correct. "If the number of atoms is N/2, the number of tetrahedral voids is N" is correct, since tetrahedral voids \(= 2 \times (N/2) = N\). The remaining option, about the centres of the spheres round an octahedral void, is discussed in the bracketed note above — as printed it is a second false statement, but the claim this question is testing, and the one the chapter's own Remember box directly refutes, is the 2N octahedral-voids claim.

Hence the statement that is not correct is that N atoms give 2N octahedral voids.

Number of atoms in 0.5 mol \(= 0.5 \times N_A = 0.5 \times 6.022 \times 10^{23} = 3.011 \times 10^{23}\).

By the Remember box in §1.6.3, for N particles the number of octahedral voids is N and the number of tetrahedral voids is 2N. Hence

octahedral voids \(= 3.011 \times 10^{23}\)

tetrahedral voids \(= 2 \times 3.011 \times 10^{23} = 6.022 \times 10^{23}\)

The question asks for octahedral **and then** tetrahedral, in that order.

Why the other three fail: one option gives exactly these two values in the reversed order (tetrahedral first), which answers a different question; the remaining two contain values \(4.011 \times 10^{23}\), \(2.011 \times 10^{23}\), \(6.011 \times 10^{23}\) and \(12.022 \times 10^{23}\), none of which is \(0.5\,N_A\) or \(N_A\), so neither can arise from 0.5 mol of substance.

Hence the numbers are \(3.011 \times 10^{23}\) and \(6.022 \times 10^{23}\) respectively.

The printed label is preserved and the reference is written "vii-b" here only so that the two items can be told apart. The question itself is unaffected.]

For an fcc unit cell the corner particles touch the face-centre particle along the face diagonal, so \(4r = \sqrt{2}\,a\) and \(r = 0.3535\,a\) (§1.7.3, Table 1.3).

With \(a = 495\ \mathrm{pm}\):

\(r = 0.3535 \times 495\ \mathrm{pm} = 175.0\ \mathrm{pm}\)

Why the other three fail: 205 pm and 260 pm both exceed \(a/2 = 247.5\ \mathrm{pm}\) or approach it so closely that the spheres would overlap along the cube edge, and neither is \(0.3535a\); 185 pm would require \(r/a = 0.374\), which is not the fcc ratio (it is not \(\sqrt{3}/4 = 0.433\), the bcc ratio, either, so it corresponds to no cubic lattice at all). Only 175 pm reproduces \(r = \sqrt{2}a/4\).

Hence the radius of the Pb atom is 175 pm.
